A novel method of creating machine learning-based time series
meta-models for building energy analysis

abstract
The meta-models have been widely used to replace computationally expensive engineering-based build-
ing energy models for model calibration, sensitivity analysis, and performance optimization of buildings.
However, most meta-models are used for monthly or annual building energy analysis applying the same
procedure as building energy or load prediction. A few studies thoroughly explore the characteristics of
meta-models when creating hourly machine learning-based meta-models for building energy assessment,
which is very different from conventional building load or energy prediction. Therefore, this paper pro-
poses a new method of creating time series models for building energy analysis based on machine learn-
ing techniques. The main feature of this new method is to include two steps (model preselection and data
folding) by taking advantage of the sequential nature during the process of constructing meta-models. A
case study of ofﬁce buildings is used to demonstrate the application of this new approach using the
EnergyPlus program and R computational environment. The results indicate that the time-series meta-
models constructed using this new method have very high accuracy with a moderate computational cost.
For the best models, the R
2 values are above 0.99 and the CV(RMSE) (coefﬁcient variation of root mean
square error) values are below 0.06 for both heating and cooling energy prediction. The ensemble
machine learning models, including Cubist, gradient boosting machine, and stacking, are recommended
to create the meta-models for hourly building energy analysis. The distributed lag models combined with
these ensemble models can be used to utilize the time-series features of hourly building energy assess-
ment. The method proposed here can be extended to the time-series energy analysis in different time
scales (sub-hourly, hourly, or daily) for other energy systems (such as PV, solar thermal, and wind).

1. Introduction
The building sector accounts for one-third of total global ﬁnal
energy and approximately 15 % of direct carbon emissions [1].
Hence, it is necessary to reduce energy and associated emissions
from buildings. The construction of building energy models can
provide insight into the building energy’s characteristics and assess
retroﬁt energy savings or carbon emission reduction in buildings.
The building energy models can be divided into the forward and
data-driven approaches [2]. The forward approach is to estimate
energy performance based on the known parameters and inputs
by using engineering-based models [3,4], such as EnergyPlus, DeST,
and DOE-2. In contrast, the data-driven approach can create a
mathematical model based on the known inputs and known out-
puts by using a number of regression methods, such as multiple

The meta-models (also named surrogate models, or emulators)
can combine both forward and data-driven methods to create
fast-run mathematical models by replacing the engineering-
based models [7]. The meta-models are of particular interest where
expensive physics-based simulations for building energy analysis
are required for a large number of simulation runs or fast compu-
tation. The meta-models can approximate complex relationships
among inputs and outputs in dynamic physics-based energy mod-
els of buildings. A good balance should be obtained between com-
putational cost and model accuracy for meta-models. In the ﬁeld of
building energy analysis, the meta-models can be used for uncer-
tainty analysis [8], model calibration [9], sensitivity analysis [10],
performance optimization [11], and model predictive control
[12]. For two-dimensional Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis, the
meta-models should be used to replace computational expensive
energy models since a large number of simulation runs are
involved (over millions of simulations in [8]). The meta-model is
a common method to reduce computational cost in model calibra-
tion since there are over 100,000 simulation runs required to reach
the convergence of MCMC results [13]. For the variance-based glo-
bal sensitivity analysis, hundreds of thousands of simulation runs
are required to reach the convergence of sensitivity indicators,
including total and main effects in building energy assessment
[14]. Hence, the meta-models can be used to expedite sensitivity
computation by replacing the models created from the EnergyPlus,
DOE-2 or other building energy simulation programs. Different
types of surrogate models (named as black-box or data-driven
models) instead of physics-based models can be used to simulate
the dynamic characteristic of building performance when applying
model predictive control techniques in buildings [12,15]. A good
overview of application of meta-model in building energy assess-
ment is available in [7].
Machine learning techniques have been widely used to create
meta-models for building energy analysis [16–19]. Liu et al. [20]
create the MARS models based on the EnergyPlus simulation
results for campus buildings located in Tianjin, China. Then the
variance-based and predictive variable importance approaches
are implemented to determine the important factors affecting
annual carbon emissions in these campus buildings. Zhang et al.
[21] construct the hourly surrogate models for building stock using
the EnergyPlus simulation engine. The predictive accuracy of sur-
rogate models obtained is within the ASHRAE guideline for model
performance [22]. Chegari et al. [23] develop surrogate models for
annual thermal energy demand and discomfort degree-hours for
the optimization of a nearly zero energy building. The meta-
models used are multilayer feed-forward networks in which a sig-
moid function for the hidden layer and a linear function for the
output layer were used as transfer functions. Li et al. [24] explore
the performance of multi-output learning models at daily,
monthly, and annual time scales using the Bayesian adaptive spline
surface and deep neural network algorithms for an ofﬁce building
located in Tianjin, China. The results indicate that the multi-output
models coupled with principal component analysis can estimate
accurate energy use at various time scales by maintaining output
correlation among outputs. Westermann et al. [25] develop the
deep temporal convolutional neural network surrogate models
for a small H-shaped ofﬁce building in the multiple climate zones
of Canada. The output variables include annual heating, annual
cooling, and hourly heating demand. Zhu et al. [26] develop the
Cubist, MARS, and SVM machine learning models for annual and
monthly electricity and gas use in an ofﬁce building. These
machine learning models are used for sensitivity analysis and
approximate Bayesian computation in the uncertainty calibration
of building energy models. For more research on machine
learning-based building energy analysis, please refer to [27–29].
Most of the previous studies are focused on the construction of
conventional time series building energy models based on the
measurement data [30,31]. For meta-models, previous studies are
concentrated on monthly or annual building energy use [7] with
little discussion of the characteristics of meta-models. There are
only a few studies on the detailed discussion of creating the hourly
meta-model analysis of building energy by making full use of the
features of the meta-model procedure.
Therefore, the aim of this paper would propose a novel method
to create the time-series meta-models of a building based on
machine learning. An ofﬁce building is used as a case study to
demonstrate the characteristics of this new method. The output
variables are hourly heating and cooling energy obtained from
the engineering-based dynamic building energy models. The
method proposed would be easily extended to different time
scales, including sub-hourly and daily energy analyses of buildings.
The method would provide an alternative method to create time-
series meta-models for other renewable energy systems, including
photovoltaics, solar thermal system, and wind electricity.
The originality of this research lies in proposing a systemically
novel two-step method of creating machine learning-based time
series meta-models for building energy analysis. This method can
preselect the good performance models from many machine learn-
ing models by ﬁrst using a small number of data sets. The features
of the time series analysis of building energy can be considered by
taking into account the lag effect and the autoregressive method
combined with the machine learning approaches. Then the predic-
tive performance of selected models can be properly assessed by
using the data folding technique. This method can make full use
of the characteristics of meta-models to sequentially create more
training data, which is signiﬁcantly different from the conventional
building energy or load predictions.
2. Method
The procedures of a novel method of creating the time-series
meta-models of building energy can be divided into three steps
as illustrated in Fig. 1. The ﬁrst step is the data preparation to col-
late the data from the engineering-based building energy models.
This step aims to construct the data more suitable for time series
analysis of building energy. The second step is the model preselec-
tion to create a number of machine learning models by considering
the characteristics of the time series of building energy and using a
small number of data sets. Three types of models are lag-free, dis-
tributed lag, and autoregressive distributed lag models. This step
aims to select several machine learning-based time series models
with good predictive performance for a given data set. The third
step is to apply the data folding technique to assess the predictive
performance of the models obtained from the previous step using
more data created from the engineering-based building energy
models. More importantly, the stability of model performance
can be evaluated based on this data folding technique. Detailed
descriptions of this method are presented in the following sections.
2.1. Data preparation

total ﬂoor area of 3200 m
2 and a window-wall ratio of 0.4. The
thermal properties of the building envelope are compatible with
the latest standards of non-domestic buildings in China [32,33].
The internal heat gains and their hourly schedules are also
obtained from these two standards [32,33]. A fan coil system is

The third type of variables are the lagged predictors derived from
the dynamic variables listed in Table 2 . For instance, the Ta_L0

the preliminary analysis and other studies [21]. Note that the lags

expected in the hour-scale of building energy analysis. The fourth
type of variable is energy use in the autoregressive model. The
maximum lag of building energy is 4-hour based on the prelimi-

The Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) method as an efﬁcient
stratiﬁed sampling method [36] is used to obtain the input matrix.
The ﬁrst step uses LHS to obtain 20 sets of data for model preselec-
tion. The second step is to perform sequential LHS based on the
previous samplings to obtain an additional 180 sets of data, in
which 100 sets are used for data folding and 100 sets are used
for model testing, as will be described in sections 2.2 and 2.3. Then,

also obtained as listed in Table 2 . There are 20 inputs (10 static

respectively, can be obtained per year in this case study. These data
sets can be used for creating the conventional machine learning
models, i.e. the lag free models. For the distributed lag and autore-
gressive distributed lag models, the inputs would be increased
accordingly, which will be described in sections 2.2.2 and 2.2.3.
2.2. Model preselection
This step is to select the meta-models from a number of learning
models using a small amount of data. The speciﬁc data size used in
this step depends on several factors, including accuracy require-
ment, time limit, and project cost. The 20 annual data sets are used
in this case study based on a preliminary study. Three types of time
series models are considered, including lag-free, distributed-lag,
and autoregressive distributed lag models. These three types of
models would be described in detail in the following three
subsections.
2.2.1. Lag-free models
The lag-free models refer to the conventional machine learning
models without considering the lagged predictors or responses.
The predictors in the lag-free models include 10 static variables
as listed in Table 1 and 10 dynamic variables as listed in Table 2 .
The detailed descriptions of these 20 predictors have been
described in section 2.1. The lag-free hourly models used in this
study can predict 8760 hourly heating and cooling energy use for
every combination of 10 static predictors. Hence, the lag-free mod-
els are different from the conventional 1-hour or 24-hour ahead
models because there is no energy use measured at the initial point
for the lag-free models.
The ten machine learning models are used for model selection
based on the previous studies [26,37]. These ten models can be
divided into three types. The ﬁrst type of models are three conven-
tional learning models, including MLR (multiple linear regression),
MARS (multivariate adaptive regression splines), and SVM (support
vector machine). The second type of models are based on neural
networks, including ANN (artiﬁcial neural network), DNN (deep
neural network), and LSTM (long short-term memory). The third
type of models are ensemble models, including RF (random forest),
GBM, CB (cubist), and stacking models. The DNN model is created
using the R H2O environment [38]. The LSTM model is created
using the R keras package [39]. The remaining learning models
are created using the R caret package [40]. The tuning parameters
are determined using the 10-fold cross-validation by considering
the bias-variance trade-off [41].
(1) The multiple linear regression model (MLR) is the simplest
model using the least square algorithm. The full linear models
without the shrinkage methods (such as ridge and step-wise
regression) are used in this case study.
(2) The MARS model is an extension of the stepwise linear
model by using piecewise linear basis functions. Then these basis
functions are used as input predictors instead of original inputs.
Two parameters should be tuned: nprune and degree. The nprune
refers to the maximum number of terms (including the intercept)
as an upper bound of model size. The degree is the maximum
degree of interaction. If the degree is 1, the models are simpliﬁed

(3) The SVM model is similar to the robust regression that
would be less affected by outliers. Two tuning parameters are cost
and sigma. The cost is the main tuning parameter to change the
model complexity by penalizing large residuals. A larger cost
parameter denotes a more ﬂexible model (likely to over-ﬁt),
whereas a smaller cost parameter denotes a more that will more
likely to under-ﬁt and less likely to over-ﬁt. The sigma is the tuning
parameter in the radial basis function kernel used in this SVM
regression.
(4) The ANN model used here is a simple feed-forward neural
network with a single hidden layer. There are two parameters to
be tuned: size and decay. The size is the number of hidden units
in the single hidden layer. The decay is to regularize the model
for moderating the over-ﬁtting. As the weight decay increases,
the regression model becomes less likely to be overﬁtting.
(5) The DNN used here is one of the deep neural networks to
refer to a multi-layer feedforward artiﬁcial neural network with
stochastic gradient descent using back propagation. Note that the
ANN model used in this paper refers to a classical neural network
with three layers (input, hidden, and output), while the DNN model
used here belongs to the deep neural networks with a large num-
ber of hidden layers. The DNN model is obtained in the H2O envi-
ronment, an open-source and scalable artiﬁcial intelligence
platform. There are a large number of parameters that can be tuned
in the DNN model, including adaptive rate, activation function, hid-
den layer & unit, L1 regularization, L2 regularization, and weight
decay.
(6) The LSTM model is one of the recurrent neural networks in
which the inputs are a sequence, such as time-series data. Hence,
the LSTM is suitable for the construction of hourly building energy
models. The LSTM models used in this section are regarded as one
of lag-free models since the input variables in previous hours are
not taken into account. The LSTM models with the previous input
variables will be considered in sections 2.2.2 and 2.2.3 as two types
of distributed lag models. The LSTM can avoid the vanishing gradi-
ent problem from the traditional recurrent neural networks since
the LSTM allows gradients to ﬂow unchanged. LSTM includes dense
layers and LSTM layer. The dense layer only accepts and processes
the simple vector data in the two-dimensional tensor, which is
called the fully connected layer. The LSTM layer is a recurrence
layer responsible for processing sequence data in a three-
dimensional tensor. The hyperparameters include the number of
units, activation function, and epochs. A hidden unit is an artiﬁcial
neuron of a hidden layer and the number of units is the number of
these hidden units in each layer of a deep learning model. The acti-
vation function in a neural network describes how the weighted
sum of the inputs could be converted into outputs in a layer of
the neural network. The epoch is the number of iterations or passes
over the training dataset.
(7) The RF model is one of the bagging methods to improve the
performance of tree-based regression. A random sample of the pre-
dictors is chosen from the full predictors to reduce correlations
among trees. There is only one hyper-parameter for the RF model
(mtry), which is the number of randomly selected predictors.
(8) The GBM model is a generalization of the tree boosting
method to improve prediction performance. Four tuning parame-
ters in the GBM model are n.trees, interaction.depth, shrinkage,
and n.minobsinnode. The n.trees is the number of boosting interac-
tions. The interaction.depth is the maximum depth of each tree.
The interaction.depth of 1 denotes an additive model and the inter-
action.depth of 2 denotes a model with 1-way interaction. The
shrinkage is also called learning rate or step-size reduction to reg-
ularize the regression model. The n.minobsinnode is the minimal
number of observations in the terminal nodes of the trees.
(9) The cubist model is a rule-based model using a method sim-
ilar to boosting learning algorithms [42]. Two parameters need to
be tuned: committees and neighbors. The committees are the
number of committees (i.e. boosting iterations) to create a
sequence of rule-based models in which the current model is
affected by the previous model. The neighbors are the number of
instances to adjust the rule-based predictions. Note that the deter-
mination of committees is not linked to the choice of instances.
(10) The stacking model is one of the ensemble methods to
combine several learning models to obtain better results than
one single learning model [43]. Firstly, the individual machine
learning models (called the ﬁrst-level models) are created using
the available data. Secondly, the predictions from these individual
machine learning models are used as inputs to create a combiner
algorithm based on the speciﬁc methods (called the second-level
models), usually simple models, such as linear regression. The ﬁrst
level models are the RF, GBM, and CB, while the second level model
is the linear regression to avoid overﬁtting in this research. The
choice of ﬁrst-level models is dependent on the accuracy and com-
putational cost of learning models.
The concise descriptions of these ten models are presented
above in this section. For more information on deep learning mod-
els, please refer to [44,45]. For detailed information on other learn-
ing models used in this research, please refer to [41,46].
2.2.2. Distributed lag models
The distributed lag (DL) models mean that the energy use of
buildings would depend on the current and past values of input
variables [47]
. These past inputs are also called lagged variables.
As a result, the distributed lag models would use the lagged predic-
tors as inputs in creating regression models [48]. The predictors for
the distributed lag models with a lag number of 1 include 10 static
variables ( Table 1 ), 10 dynamic variables ( Table 2 ), and 9 lagged
predictors except for day type ( Table 2). Hence, the number of pre-
dictors would increase to 29 for the one lag model. Note that the
day type would change in the time scale of day and there is no
new variable of day type for the lagged models in the hourly time
scale. For the 2-hour lag model, extra 9 predictors in the previous
two hours (except for day type in Table 2 ) will be added to the
model besides 29 predictors for the 1-hour lag model. The same
principle can be applied to the 3-hour and 4-hour lag models. If
the lag number is increased to 4, then the number of predictors
becomes 56, around 3 times the lag-free models. For learning mod-
els, more predictors would require more computational time.
Hence, the best three models selected from the lag-free models
would be used to create the distributed lag models for both hourly
heating and cooling energy of buildings in this case study.
Fig. 3 illustrates the computational procedures for the dis-
tributed 3-hour lag models for both heating and cooling energy
use of buildings. The building energy at 8:00 on a given day should
be ﬁrstly predicted since the HVAC system would be turned on at
8:00. The inputs include static parameters and dynamic parame-
ters. The static parameters are 10 factors as listed in Table 1 . The
dynamic parameters at 8:00 are 10 factors as listed in Table 1 .I n
addition, the dynamic parameters from 5:00 to 7:00 should be also
considered due to being a 3-hour lag model. These inputs are
entered into the machine learning-based distributed lag model to
obtain the energy use at 8:00. The same procedure is also used
from 9:00 to 18:00 on a given day. Then the hourly energy use of
a building in one year can be predicted from the distributed 3-
hour lag models.
2.2.3. Autoregressive distributed lag models
The autoregressive distributed lag (ADL) models [49] would
assume that building energy use would depend on both lagged

dependent and lagged independent variables. The autoregressive
term means the past outputs would also affect the current outputs
besides the input variables [47]. Hence, the ADL model would
include the lagged dependent and lagged input variables as predic-
tors. The ADL1 refers to the ADL model with one lag. For the ADL1
model, the predictors include 10 static variables ( Table 1 ), 10
dynamic variables ( Table 2 ), 9 lagged predictors except for day
type ( Table 2 ), and energy use in the previous hour. As a result,
the total number of predictors is 30 for the ADL1 model. The same
procedure can be applied to other ADL models. Thus, the ADL4
models have 60 predictors since there are 56 inputs plus 4 energy
data among the previous 4 h. Note that the previous-hour energy is
required for the ADL model. The determination of previous-hour
energy data as predictors would be discussed in the following
paragraph.
Fig. 4 illustrates the computational steps for the autoregressive
3-hour lag models applicable to both the heating and cooling
energy of buildings. The energy use at 8:00 would be ﬁrstly com-
puted since the HVAC system would be switched on at 8:00. There
are three types of input data. The ﬁrst type of data are the static
parameters as listed in Table 1 . The second type of data are the
dynamic parameters in the current hour (8:00) and the previous
3 h (5:00–7:00). The third type of data are the 3-hour previous
energy use from 5:00 to 7:00. These energy data would be taken
as zero since the HVAC system has been turned off during these
three hours. These input data are entered into the autoregressive
distributed lag models to obtain the energy use at 8:00. The same
procedure can be applied for the prediction of energy use at 9:00.
Note that the energy use at 8:00 as one of the inputs is based on
the computed value in the last step, but cannot be taken as zero
in the case of the computation of energy use at 9:00. This proce-
dure can be used to obtain the hourly energy use from 8:00 to
18:00.
2.3. Data folding
The data folding technique is used to provide a robust estima-
tion of predictive performance from the models selected in the pre-
vious step. The data folding method used in this step is different
from the conventional cross-validation [50]. The variable impor-
tance would be applied to determine the most important variable
affecting building energy use [51]. Then this key variable would be
used in the process of data folding analysis to produce a more bal-
anced training set for creating reliable building energy models. The
training set would be partitioned into k sets of roughly equal size.
The k value would be changed from 1 to 5, which indicates that dif-
ferent sizes of training data sets would be created to assess the sta-
bility of predictive performance. The ﬁve different sizes are 1/5,
1/4, 1/3, 1/2, and 1 of the whole training set. The corresponding
sizes of ﬁve data sets are 20, 25, 33, 50, and 100 in this case study.
Hence, the change in the predictive performance of the learning
models created from different data sizes would be evaluated to
provide more robust results. Moreover, this process can be used
to choose more accurate learning models from several models
selected in the stage of model preselection as described in section
2.2. The process described in this paper has the advantage of being
sequential in both two steps. In the step of model pre-selection,
several accurate models can be chosen using a small number of
data. In the step of data folding, the predictive performance of
these models chosen from the ﬁrst step would be assessed by using
the data set with an increase in data size. This process is in line
with the features of meta-models, which can create the extra train-
ing data set by running the engineering-based building energy
models more times.

The tuning process can provide useful information on the char-
acteristics of building energy use. This section is focused on the
tuning process for the lag-free learning models. Table 3 lists the
ﬁnal tuning parameters from ten lag-free machine learning mod-
els. Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 show the tuning process for the GBM and RF
models, respectively.
Table 3 lists the optimal tuning parameters from the ten lag-
free machine learning models for heating and cooling energy. The
meanings of these tuning parameters have been described in sec-
tion 2.2.1. The differences in these parameters are not signiﬁcant
between heating and cooling energy in this case study. Hence,
the model complexity for estimating heating and cooling energy
is similar. For the MLR models, there is no parameter to be tuned.
For the MARS model, the ﬁnal tuning parameters are the same for
both the heating and cooling energy of the building. For the SVM
model, the cost parameter for cooling energy is higher than that
for heating energy. As a result, more complex SVM models are
required for cooling energy compared to heating energy. For three
neural network models, the differences in parameters are small
between the heating and cooling energy of buildings. Note that
the tuning processes for the DNN and LSTM models are much more
difﬁcult and time-consuming in comparison with the conventional
ANN. The computational cost of these learning models would be
discussed in sections 3.2 and 3.3. For the ensemble models, the
parameters are still very similar between heating and cooling
energy models. The tuning process for the GBM and RF models
would be described in the following paragraph. For the CB models,
the ﬁnal parameters are the same as for the heating and cooling
energy models. For stacking models, the linear model is used in
the second layer to reduce overﬁtting.
For the GBM models, the cross-validation RMSE of both heating
and cooling energy would be decreased with an increase in boost-
ing iterations as shown in Fig. 5. The RMSE would be also reduced
with an increase in interaction depth. Hence, a sufﬁcient number of
trees is necessary to improve model predictive performance. There
exist the complex interactions of predictors, which can be con-
ﬁrmed with the degree parameter of MARS models as listed in
Table 3. For the RF models, the cross-validation RMSE errors would
be decreased with an increase of randomly selected predictors as
shown in Fig. 6 . After the predictor numbers further increase, the
RMSE values would become stable. More predictors are required
for the heating energy model compared to the cooling energy
model in this case study.
The tuning parameters are discussed for the lag free models.
However, it is found that the ﬁnal tuning parameters in most of
the learning models are the same between the lag-free models,
the distributed lagged models, and the autoregressive distributed
lag models. Hence, the discussion on the other two models would
not be presented. More computational cost is required for the two
lagged models by considering the lagged effects of both inputs and
outputs. Therefore, the ranges of tuning parameters in these two
types of models can be reduced based on the tuning results from
the lag-free models. This would expedite the computational pro-
cess of creating reliable meta-models for building energy analysis.

3.5. Practical advice in the construction of building energy time series
meta-models
This section discusses the practical advice for creating machine
learning-based time series meta-models in building energy analy-
sis. The topics include the generality of the method proposed, the
choice of time series models, the difference between conventional
data-driven models and meta-models, the use of sequential fea-
tures in meta-model construction, the choice of learning models,
and the application of hourly meta-models.
The method illustrated in Fig. 1 can be applied to the different
buildings in various locations due to its good generality although
this method is demonstrated by a case study as described in sec-
tion 2.1. The generality of the method mainly includes the choice
of learning models and the selection of time features of time series
models. The choice of lag-free methods can be easily expanded by
adding more new and advanced machine learning algorithms to
increase the predictive capability of models except for ten learning
models used in section 2.2.1. The different time features of energy
use in buildings are considered, including lag-free, distributed lag,
and autoregressive distributed lag models. Hence, the models cre-
ated here can be more suitable for predicting energy use in differ-
ent buildings.
It is necessary to explore the characteristics of (autoregressive)
distributed lag models in creating time series building energy
models. The predictive performance of lag-free models should be
ﬁrst evaluated since they are fast run due to the fewer input num-
bers in comparison with the (autoregressive) distributed lag mod-
els. The distributed lag models would perform better compared to
the autoregressive distributed lag models due to the accumulative
errors of autoregressive models. If the project is limited by the time
and computational cost, the lag free and distributed lag machine
learning models can be applied in constructing building energy
models. The lag number can be also explored using the cross-
validation technique. The higher lag number over four is unlikely
to be useful to improve the predictive performance in creating
meta-models for building energy analysis.
The difference between conventional load/energy prediction
and meta-models can be summarized from four aspects: input
determination, data availability, data quality, and initial data.
There are signiﬁcant differences in how to specify input variables

between conventional load/energy prediction and meta-models.
The conventional data-driven models can be regarded as ex-ante
forecasts [54]. The predictors should be estimated in the ex-ante
forecast in building energy prediction. As a result, the predictors
that are hard to predict should be excluded. For instance, occu-
pancy behaviors have important inﬂuences on building loads [55]
but are difﬁcult to accurately forecast due to the inherent high
uncertainty. In contrast, the meta-models of building energy anal-
ysis can be considered as the ex-post forecast in which the predic-
tors are known [54]. Hence, the variables inﬂuencing building
energy (including occupant behavior) can be added to the meta-
models of building energy. The second aspect is data availability
between conventional load/energy prediction and meta-models.
For conventional load/energy prediction, the data are hard to be
changed for a speciﬁc building. In contrast, the extra new data
are easily created using the physics-based building energy models
for the meta-model construction. The effects of data availability
would be discussed in the following paragraph. The third aspect
is that the data quality from the conventional load or energy pre-
diction of buildings should be carefully checked [56], whereas
there are no data quality issues in the meta-models of building
energy. The fourth aspect is about the initial data at the current
time. For the conventional load/energy prediction, the initial data
is the energy use measured at the current time. The 1-hour or
24-hour ahead prediction can be conducted based on this initial
data. For the meta-models, there are no initial data since there
are no measurement data. If energy use is regarded as an input
variable, there are different ways to create this initial data. The initial
energy use can be regarded as zero if the HVAC system is turned off at
a speciﬁc time. If the initial energy use is not zero, then the initial
energy data can be estimated by running the ﬁrst-day simulation
several times to check the stability of energy results.
One of the differences between load/energy prediction and
meta-model construction of buildings is the data availability as dis-
cussed in the previous paragraph. It is much easier to create data
from engineering-based building energy models. Hence, the con-
struction of time series meta-models should take advantage of this
feature to implement the multi-step procedure. For instance, the
model performance from ten (maybe more) machine learning
models can be ﬁrstly assessed from a small number of data using
cross-validation. This step is necessary because the construction
of machine learning models is very time-consuming for deep learn-
ing models and some ensemble learning models. Moreover, the
prediction time is also long for some autoregressive meta-models
since it is almost impossible to use parallel computation because
the energy used in the latter hour depends on the previous hours.
The several learning models with better performance can be cho-
sen from the preselection procedure to be further assessed using
more large data. The method proposed here has a good sequential
feature to be more suitable for the construction of reliable time
series meta-models in buildings.
The choice of machine learning models for creating meta-
models in buildings should be balanced between prediction capa-
bility and computational cost. In terms of prediction capability,
the deep learning models and the ensemble models have good per-
formance. The deep learning models are usually more time-

The hourly meta-models developed from this research can be

the optimization of heating systems, demand response, model cal-

models of building components and subsystems, especially HVAC
systems, are often required to be calibrated based on hourly or
sub-hourly data [9]. The hourly meta-models obtained in this paper
are more easily combined with the ABC method [26] for the model
calibration of building energy models, compared with the individ-
ual models at the different hour scales. Besides, the building hourly
meta-model can also reduce the energy consumption of building
operations while ensuring the thermal comfort of indoor occupants
by optimizing multiple target parameters, such as HVAC set-point
temperature, lamp, and equipment utilization rate [57,58]. The
application of meta-models for building performance optimization
has the advantage of signiﬁcant time savings over physical simula-
tion models.
4. Conclusion
This paper explores the construction of fast and accurate time-
series meta-models to replace the engineering-based building
energy model. The following conclusions can be obtained from this
research.
(1) A novel method has been proposed to create machine
learning-based time series meta-models for assessing building
energy performance. The main steps include data preparation,
model preselection, and data folding. The data preparation is to
prepare the data suitable for time series analysis. The model selec-
tion can choose the learning models with good predictive perfor-
mance and moderate computational cost from a number of
machine learning models using a small amount of data. The data
folding can assess the predictive performance of learning models
chosen from the previous step to provide a robust evaluation of
model performance.
(2) The distributed lag models perform well in creating time
series meta-models of building energy. The predictive performance
of autoregressive distributed lag models should be carefully
assessed due to the accumulative errors from the estimation of
energy use in previous hours.
(3) Computational time for the building energy meta-models
should be carefully checked, especially for autoregressive models,
because the computational time is the key advantage for meta-
models to replace the engineering-based building energy models.
The prediction of energy use should be used as input predictors
in predicting the building energy use in the next hour for the
autoregressive time series models. Then it is hard to apply parallel
computing to expedite the computation in this case.
(4) The accuracy of time-series meta-models in building energy
analysis does not necessarily increase with an increase in data size.
Hence, it is necessary to check the stability of model accuracy. The
data folding technique combined with variable importance can be
used to provide robust analysis to this end.
(5) The ensemble machine learning methods perform well,
including Cubist, GBM, and stacking, in terms of predictive capabil-
ity and computational cost. These methods can be used for creating
reliable time-series building energy meta-models. The deep learn-
ing methods have good predictive performance at the expense of
high computational cost and high tuning parameter efforts. For
the optimal models for both heating and cooling energy prediction
from this research, the R
2 values are above 0.99 and the CV(RMSE)
(coefﬁcient variation of root mean square error) values are less
than 0.06.
(6) The method proposed here can be easily combined with the
sequential sampling methods to provide more accurate meta-
models by incrementally adding more data sets. These sequential
features can make full use of the characteristics of meta-models,
which can more easily add training data sets. Hence, the method
proposed here can achieve a good balance between model accuracy
and computational cost.
This research is only applied to an ofﬁce building in Tianjin,
China. More building types in various locations should be explored
to assess time series features in creating time series meta-models
for building energy assessment. Note that the method proposed
in this research can be easily extended for different time steps of
building energy analysis, such as sub-hourly, daily, and weekly.
Another interesting area is to explore prediction intervals for the
machine learning-based time series models of building energy.
Moreover, the models developed in this analysis should be applied
in model calibration, sensitivity analysis, optimization, and model
predictive control at short-time intervals to evaluate their suitabil-
ity in different contexts of building energy assessment.
